notes.b: A policy is a government's written plan for what it wants to achieve and how. Ireland has three national policies that aim to get more people active, and each one has a slightly different focus.
points: The National Physical Activity Plan for Ireland, published in 2016, is the government's plan to increase physical activity levels across the whole population, with actions across health, education, transport, sport and communities.
The National Sports Policy 2018–2027 is the government's ten-year policy to increase sport participation, develop high performance (the top level of elite sport) and improve sports facilities.
Healthy Ireland is the government framework (an overall structure that guides other plans) to improve the health and wellbeing of the population, including through physical activity.
notes.tip: Healthy Ireland, the National Physical Activity Plan and the National Sports Policy are all acceptable answers when asked to name a national policy. Do not invent others.

notes.h: National and local bodies and local actions
notes.b: Policies only work if someone delivers them. Sport Ireland does this nationally, Local Sports Partnerships do it in each area, and councils, schools and clubs add their own local plans.
points: Sport Ireland is the statutory body (one set up by law) responsible for developing sport in Ireland. It was established in 2015 under the Sport Ireland Act 2015, replacing the Irish Sports Council.
Sport Ireland funds national governing bodies and Local Sports Partnerships, runs participation programmes and anti-doping, and supports high performance.
Local Sports Partnerships (LSPs) are local bodies in counties and cities, funded by Sport Ireland, that increase participation at local level.
LSPs focus on under-represented groups, meaning people who take part less than others, and work through local programmes, coach education, community events and information.
County council recreation and active-travel plans provide greenways, parks and cycle lanes, so people have safe, free places to be active close to home.
School physical activity policies set out how the school provides PE and activity, so every pupil has a regular chance to be active.
Club development plans set out how a club will grow its membership and coaching.
notes.tip: Do not quote the number of LSPs or funding figures. Name Sport Ireland, say what it funds, and say that LSPs work locally with under-represented groups.

notes.b: To analyse a policy, look at its aims, its actions, who it targets, and its strengths and limitations. The example here is the National Physical Activity Plan for Ireland.
points: Aim: to increase physical activity levels across the population.
Actions: set out across health, education, transport, sport and communities.
Target: the whole population, so several sectors of society have a role in carrying it out.
Strength: it coordinates action across government sectors, so health, education and transport are linked in one plan.
Strength: a national framework gives local bodies a shared direction, so their work pulls the same way.
Limitation: its actions depend on each sector implementing them, so gaps in implementation slow progress.
Limitation: funding gaps can stop local actions from going ahead.
Limitation: many local activities rely on volunteers, which limits how far they can grow.
notes.tip: When asked to name a policy and analyse how it promotes activity, give its aim, the actions it sets out and who it targets, then add at least one strength and one limitation with a reason.

notes.b: A national governing body (NGB) governs one sport or activity in Ireland and is linked to the international federation for that sport. It is the organisation that keeps the sport running and growing.
points: Sets and enforces the rules of the sport, so every club plays the same game fairly.
Organises competitions, such as national leagues and championships.
Develops coaches and officials through education and certification, so people are trained to a recognised standard.
Supports clubs, which are where most people actually take part.
Selects and prepares national teams.
Promotes participation through programmes and campaigns.
Links the sport to the international federation that governs it internationally.

notes.b: Most people meet their NGB through a local club, school or league. This is where the NGB does most of its work to get people started and keep them playing.
points: Affiliates clubs (admits them as members) and gives them governance, insurance, safeguarding policies (rules that protect children and vulnerable people) and codes of conduct.
Educates coaches, officials and first-aiders, so sessions are well run and safe.
Development officers visit schools to run introductory sessions and link pupils to local clubs, so a first taste of the sport leads to regular membership.
Local leagues and blitzes (short tournaments in which many teams play one day) give beginners regular, low-pressure games.
Grants for facilities and equipment reduce the cost and access barriers to joining a club.
Extra funding can pay for more development officers and participation programmes.
Extra funding can also improve facilities, deliver coach education and run campaigns.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to name an NGB and examine how it supports local participation, to suggest three ways it can promote activity locally, or to describe what it could do with extra funding. Pick distinct points such as school visits, local leagues and grants, and say how each gets people involved.

notes.h: NGB support at national and international level
notes.b: Beyond local clubs, an NGB runs the national structure of its sport and represents Ireland internationally.
points: It runs national competitions and leagues under the sport's rules.
It operates disciplinary systems for breaches of the rules, so the rules are enforced fairly.
It builds national coaching structures that develop coaches at each level.
It provides talent pathways and development squads for young players, so promising players are noticed and developed.
It sets safeguarding standards that apply to every club and member.
It holds membership of an international federation, which sets international rules for the sport.
It selects and prepares national teams for international competition.
It hosts international events, and implements international rules and anti-doping.
notes.tip: Keep the international role to membership of the federation, teams, events, rules and anti-doping. Pathways to excellence and high-performance support belong to the next subsection.

notes.h: Named NGBs: Gaelic games and team sports
notes.b: You need to be able to name the governing body for common activities. These are the NGBs for the main team sports.
points: GAA: Gaelic football and hurling.
Camogie Association: camogie.
Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA): ladies' Gaelic football.
Football Association of Ireland (FAI): association football.
Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU): rugby union.
Basketball Ireland: basketball.
Hockey Ireland: hockey.
notes.tip: If asked to name two other NGBs and their sports, always pair the body with its sport, for example the FAI with association football.

notes.b: These are the NGBs for individual and other sports. Note that one body can govern several related activities.
points: Athletics Ireland: athletics.
Swim Ireland: swimming, water polo, diving and artistic swimming in Ireland.
Badminton Ireland: badminton.
Tennis Ireland: tennis.
Gymnastics Ireland: gymnastics.
Rowing Ireland: rowing.

notes.h: Tip sheet: target group and promotion tips
notes.b: A tip sheet names one target group, gives promotion tips to attract them and adherence tips (covered next) to keep them taking part, and justifies each tip for that group.
points: Target group: choose one specific group, such as teenage girls, older adults, office workers or beginners returning after a long absence, so every tip can be matched to their needs.
Promotion: start small with short, easy sessions, because a modest first step feels manageable and is more likely to be repeated.
Promotion: choose enjoyable activities, since people keep doing what they enjoy.
Promotion: exercise with friends or in a group, because shared activity adds social motivation.
Promotion: schedule activity like an appointment, so it is planned rather than left to chance.
Promotion: set a clear first goal, such as attending one session each week, so early success is visible from the start.
Promotion: use free local options such as parkrun, walking routes and greenways, which remove cost as a barrier.
notes.tip: Every tip must be justified for your chosen group: say why it helps that group start. A tip with no reason, or a reason that suits everyone, loses the mark.

notes.b: Adherence means sticking with activity over weeks and months, not just starting. These tips help a target group keep going once the first enthusiasm fades.
points: Set SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound), so progress can be judged and goals stay realistic.
Track progress with an app or diary, so improvement is visible and motivation holds.
Vary activities, which prevents boredom and reduces overuse injuries.
Reward milestones, so each achievement gives a reason to continue.
Plan for barriers such as bad weather or lack of time, with an indoor option or a shorter session, so one bad week does not end the habit.
Build up gradually to avoid injury and soreness, which can make people stop.
Join a club or class for social support, which gives people a commitment to others.
notes.tip: A common question asks for two adherence tips for someone returning after a long absence, each justified. Building up gradually and planning for barriers suit this group well, and you must say why each helps them keep going.

notes.b: Significant people are those whose influence shapes whether someone takes part. They include parents and family, PE teachers, coaches, peers, local club volunteers, sports stars and role models. The characteristics below make them effective.
points: Enthusiastic and passionate about activity, which spreads to the people they work with.
Lead by example by being active themselves, so their actions match their words.
Positive and encouraging, which builds confidence in people who doubt their ability.
Approachable and supportive, so people feel comfortable asking for help.
Knowledgeable about the activity and about how to teach or coach it safely.
Inclusive and fair to all abilities, so everyone feels welcome.
Reliable and committed, so people can count on them to turn up.
Good communicators who explain clearly and give useful feedback.
Visible and relatable to the target group, so people see someone like themselves taking part.
notes.tip: When asked for two characteristics, name each one and explain its effect on the person being supported, for example that encouragement builds confidence. For a case study, pick characteristics the person in it clearly shows.

notes.b: A role model is someone admired whom others copy. Their influence reaches beyond the people who know them personally.
points: Role models inspire people to try an activity they might not otherwise consider.
Role models show that taking part is possible for 'people like me', so people can believe they could do it too.
Role models raise the profile of a sport and bring it to the attention of new players and families.

keyTerms.definition: A body established by law, with duties set out in legislation.
The statutory body responsible for developing sport in Ireland, which funds national governing bodies and Local Sports Partnerships.
A Sport Ireland-funded local body in a county or city that increases participation locally, especially among under-represented groups.
The organisation that governs a sport or activity in a country, setting rules, organising competitions and developing coaches and officials.
The formal link between a club and its national governing body, which gives the club governance, insurance and access to the body's programmes.
A person who works with schools and clubs to grow participation in a sport.
A short, informal day of games or competition, often for beginners or young players, held at local level.
The governing body for one sport at international level, which sets international rules and organises international competition.
Continuing to take part in physical activity over time.
Goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
A person who influences others' participation in physical activity, such as a parent, teacher, coach or role model.
The specific group of people that a promotion or tip sheet is designed to reach.

Swimming, water polo, diving and artistic swimming in Ireland.

factCards.term: Three ways an NGB can promote participation locally

questions.prompt: Name a national policy that promotes physical activity and analyse how it promotes physical activity engagement.
questions.model: The National Physical Activity Plan for Ireland, published in 2016, aims to increase physical activity levels across the population. It promotes engagement by setting out actions across health, education, transport, sport and communities, so more people are encouraged to be active in settings such as school, work and their local area. Its cross-sector approach is a strength, because coordinated action across government sectors can reach people in several settings at once, and a shared national framework gives local bodies such as clubs, schools and councils a common direction. Its limitations are that delivery depends on each sector implementing its actions, so gaps in implementation or funding can slow progress locally, and many community actions rely on volunteers, which limits how far they can expand.

questions.prompt: Discuss how a named National Governing Body supports the development of its sport at local level.
questions.model: The GAA, the governing body for Gaelic football and hurling, supports development at local level in several ways. It affiliates clubs and gives them governance, insurance, safeguarding policies and codes of conduct, so clubs can run safely and to a common standard. It educates coaches, officials and first-aiders, so each club has people able to teach and officiate. Development officers work with schools and clubs to introduce pupils to the games and link them to local clubs. Local leagues and blitzes give beginners and young players regular, low-pressure games that keep them involved. Grants for facilities and equipment reduce the cost barrier, so clubs can improve their grounds and buy kit. Together these supports build the club base from which players progress.

questions.prompt: Outline three characteristics of significant people, such as role models, who promote participation among young people.
questions.model: 1. Enthusiastic and passionate: a significant person who is enthusiastic about activity spreads that enthusiasm to others and makes taking part appealing. 2. Leads by example: being active themselves shows young people that activity is normal and achievable. 3. Positive and encouraging: praise and support build the confidence of young people who doubt their own ability, so they keep trying.
